analysis.one_liner: Hands governors veto power over endangered species listings and pays landowners 150% of property value when protections cost them money.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate on November 19, 2013, referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act so that no species could be listed as endangered or threatened without the consent of the governor of every state where it lives, and Congress would have to approve every listing by a joint resolution — with all listings expiring automatically after five years. Governors could take over protection of species found only in their state, with no court able to review their decisions. The bill would also let landowners get a quick federal ruling on whether a planned use of their property is legal (deemed legal if the government misses a 90-day deadline), force taxpayers to pay owners 150% of a property's value if protections cut its worth by half, and strip attorney fees from citizen lawsuits under the Act. It died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners, developers, and industries whose projects are constrained by endangered species protections would gain the most: a 90-day default approval for any proposed land use, a 150%-of-value payout when a protection decision cuts a property's worth by half, and a state-level veto over listings. Governors of states with one-of-a-kind species would gain exclusive regulatory power over them.

how_it_helps.text: A governor's consent would be required before any species in that state could be listed as endangered or threatened, and species found in only one state could be regulated exclusively by that state's governor, with no judicial review of the governor's decisions.
Landowners could get a binding determination on a proposed use of their property within 90 days; if the Interior Department missed the deadline, the use would be deemed legal.
If a protection decision cut a property's value by 50% or more for its intended use, the government would have to pay the owner or lessee 150% of fair market value.
Attorney-fee awards in Endangered Species Act citizen suits would be eliminated, and new listings would require an act of Congress and would expire after five years.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund 150% property-value payouts and absorb the cost of any species that loses protection when a governor withholds consent or Congress declines to renew a listing. The public would also lose citizen-suit enforcement as a check on government inaction.

drawbacks.text: A landowner's proposed use of property would automatically be deemed legal if the Interior Department missed a 90-day response deadline, creating a loophole for projects affecting habitat when the agency is backlogged.

Taxpayers would pay 150% of fair market value to any owner or lessee whose property value drops at least 50% because of a species protection decision, a payout far above standard constitutional takings compensation.
The bill eliminates citizen suits' attorney-fee awards, which has the practical effect of making it much harder for ordinary citizens to enforce species protections in court.

Every listing would expire automatically after five years, requiring fresh congressional action to keep protecting a species — a design that could drop protections for at-risk species whenever Congress is gridlocked.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered landowners and developers faster certainty and generous compensation, but its centerpiece — a 90-day default approval and 150% buyouts — would have shifted large public costs onto taxpayers, and giving a single governor veto power over national listings with no court review would have gutted a law that has prevented extinctions for decades. Weighing landowner convenience against the loss of a functioning national safety net for species, the costs outweighed the benefits. In any case, it was never seriously considered.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee from the day it was introduced in November 2013 until Congress ended in January 2015, without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Rand Paul on November 19, 2013, with two Republican cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day — the only action it ever received.
The committee never reported the bill and no chamber ever voted on it before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing endangered species protections stayed fully in place; the bill's supporters in development and industry avoided nothing because nothing happened, while species and their habitats remained protected.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and advocated its landowner-compensation and state-control provisions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only three Republican sponsors and no Democratic cosponsors; it never reached the Senate floor, so no recorded vote shows how the chamber as a whole would have split.

industries.industry: Land developers and real estate interests
industries.note: The bill gives developers a 90-day default approval for any proposed land use and a 150% payout if species protections cut their property value in half, both of which lower the cost and risk of building in species habitat. It also strips attorney fees from citizen suits, reducing the legal threat of environmental challenges.

Federal power administrators would have to itemize Endangered Species Act compliance costs on customer bills, a transparency measure aimed at building political pressure against species-protecting operations like dam flow restrictions.

The bill removes their main enforcement tool — citizen suits with fee recovery — and eliminates the citizen petition process for listing species, sharply reducing their ability to compel government action. The public loses a mechanism for protecting species in the process.

Governors would gain a veto over federal listings in their state and exclusive authority over species found only within their borders, shifting power from federal scientists to state politicians. Whether that helps the public depends on each governor's priorities.
